contents.text: Germany was not the only European country ruled by a totalitarian leader after World War I. Read the passage about Italy. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Italy was originally neutral in World War I. It entered the war on the side of the United Kingdom, France, and Russia in 1915 in exchange for the promise of receiving new land at the end of the war. But it received less land than promised, angering many Italians. In addition, Italy faced high unemployment, large war debts, and significant costs of rebuilding areas that had been destroyed during the war.

contents.text: In January 1941, President Roosevelt gave his State of the Union address. In the speech, he outlined a vision for the world in which all people would enjoy four freedoms: freedom of speech, freedom of worship, freedom from want, and freedom from fear. Additionally, Roosevelt made a case for increasing U.S. involvement in world events. Read the following excerpts from Roosevelt's Four Freedoms speech. Then match each excerpt to Roosevelt's purpose.

draggableItems.text: to stress the consequences of losing the war

staticItems.text: I find it, unhappily, necessary to report that the future and the safety of our country and of our democracy are overwhelmingly involved in events far beyond our borders.
Every realist knows that the democratic way of life is at this moment being directly assailed…by those who seek to destroy unity and promote discord in nations that are still at peace.

The need of the moment is that our actions and our policy should be devoted primarily—almost exclusively—to meeting this foreign peril. For all our domestic problems are now a part of the great emergency.

No realistic American can expect from a dictator's [victory] international generosity, or return of true independence, or world disarmament, or freedom of expression, or freedom of religion—or even good business. Such a peace would bring no security for us or for our neighbors.

contents.text: In January 1941, President Roosevelt gave his State of the Union address. In the speech, he outlined a vision for the world in which all people would enjoy four freedoms: freedom of speech, freedom of worship, freedom from want, and freedom from fear. Additionally, Roosevelt made a case for increasing U.S. involvement in world events. Read the following excerpts from Roosevelt's Four Freedoms speech. Then match each of Roosevelt's goals to the appropriate excerpt from his speech.

draggableItems.text: I find it, unhappily, necessary to report that the future and the safety of our country and of our democracy are overwhelmingly involved in events far beyond our borders.
Every realist knows that the democratic way of life is at this moment being directly assailed…by those who seek to destroy unity and promote discord in nations that are still at peace.

No realistic American can expect from a dictator's [victory] international generosity, or return of true independence, or world disarmament, or freedom of expression, or freedom of religion—or even good business. Such a peace would bring no security for us or for our neighbors.

The need of the moment is that our actions and our policy should be devoted primarily—almost exclusively—to meeting this foreign peril. For all our domestic problems are now a part of the great emergency.

contents.text: During the late 1930s, tensions between the United States and Japan increased. In 1937, Japan invaded China, which prompted a series of actions by the United States. Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: During the 1930s, Japan invaded China despite condemnation by the international community. In 1940, Japan expanded the invasion to French colonies in Southeast Asia. Hoping to slow Japanese war efforts, the United States implemented a trade embargo, banning the sale of certain metals and rubber to Japan.

In response to the U.S. embargo, Japan signed the Tripartite Pact, joining the Axis powers. As Japan's invasions advanced closer to U.S. territories in the Pacific, President Roosevelt extended the trade embargo to include oil. Japan's critical shortage of fuel jeopardized both its military and industrial capacity. While Japanese diplomats continued negotiations with the United States to end the embargo, Japan's leaders secretly began preparing for a possible military attack.

contents.text: In January 1941, President Roosevelt gave his State of the Union address. In the speech, he outlined a vision for the world in which all people would enjoy four freedoms: freedom of speech, freedom of worship, freedom from want, and freedom from fear. Additionally, Roosevelt made a case for increasing U.S. involvement in world events. Read the following excerpts from Roosevelt's Four Freedoms speech. Then match each excerpt to Roosevelt's purpose.

draggableItems.text: to emphasize that democratic ideals are under attack even though the United States is at peace
to reluctantly acknowledge that the United States must become more involved in international affairs to ensure its future stability
to rally Americans to prepare for the war effort with urgency
to stress the consequences of losing the war

staticItems.text: I find it, unhappily, necessary to report that the future and the safety of our country and of our democracy are overwhelmingly involved in events far beyond our borders.
Every realist knows that the democratic way of life is at this moment being directly assailed…by those who seek to destroy unity and promote discord in nations that are still at peace.

The need of the moment is that our actions and our policy should be devoted primarily—almost exclusively—to meeting this foreign peril. For all our domestic problems are now a part of the great emergency.

No realistic American can expect from a dictator's [victory] international generosity, or return of true independence, or world disarmament, or freedom of expression, or freedom of religion—or even good business. Such a peace would bring no security for us or for our neighbors.

, or "lightning war," tactics, which meant aggressively using infantry, tanks, and airplanes together. They captured over 3 million Soviet soldiers, most of whom died in captivity. Germany then turned its focus to capturing oil fields in the southern Soviet Union. This led to the

, a brutal six-month fight that destroyed the city and claimed millions of lives in urban warfare. By autumn 1943, the German military on the Eastern Front was on the defensive and spent the rest of the war on a long retreat back to Germany.

pieces.text: Planes flew near the battlefield to help ground troops complete their missions.
Large bomber fleets flew long-distance missions to attack German factories, cities, and economic infrastructure from the air.
Unarmed or lightly armed aircraft flew over enemy territory to gather vital information and spread
, or messages designed to harm enemy morale.

contents.text: Sort the following examples by which of the above roles they fulfilled.

label.text: The 332nd Fighter Group, called the Tuskegee Airmen, escorted bombers from Italy into Germany, fighting and intercepting German planes.
Bombers flew nighttime missions over enemy territory to drop millions of paper flyers urging soldiers to surrender.
In late 1944, the 439th Troop Carrier Group dropped supplies for the 101st Airborne Division in Belgium, allowing them to hold out against German attacks.
In July 1943, C‑47 transport planes dropped thousands of troops from the 82nd Airborne Division into Sicily to aid the invasion.

Unarmed, high-speed aircraft flew thousands of missions to photograph every German bunker and obstacle in northern France.

dealt with a wide range of war-related issues and outcomes. Match each discussion topic to its outcome.

draggableItems.text: The Allies agreed that the invasion to liberate Western Europe from the Axis would begin in the spring of 1944.
The Allies agreed to give the Soviet Union land from eastern Poland, compensating Poland with new land from western Germany.

of World War II in Europe. The Soviets responded by joining the Allies in their fight against Germany. The Eastern Front was the largest front of the war and one of the deadliest in history. Over 12 million soldiers died there, and nearly twice as many civilians were killed by disease, starvation, and war crimes committed by both sides.
During the first six months, the German military used

, or "lightning war," tactics, which meant aggressively using infantry, tanks, and airplanes together. They captured over 3 million Soviet soldiers, most of whom died in captivity. German forces reached Moscow, the Soviet capital, but failed to capture the city. Both armies suffered heavy losses in the fighting.
Germany then turned its focus to capturing oil fields in the southern Soviet Union. This led to the

, a brutal six-month fight that destroyed the city and claimed millions of lives in urban warfare. The Soviet army, drawing on huge numbers of new recruits, trapped and forced the remaining members of the German 6th Army to surrender. Although Germany would later attempt other offensives, it never recovered from its catastrophic defeat at Stalingrad. By autumn 1943, the German military on the Eastern Front was on the defensive and spent the rest of the war on a long retreat back to Germany.

pieces.text: Planes flew near the battlefield to help ground troops complete their missions.
Large bomber fleets flew long-distance missions to attack German factories, cities, and economic infrastructure from the air.
Unarmed or lightly armed aircraft flew over enemy territory to gather vital information and spread
, or messages designed to harm enemy morale.

, or codebreakers, decoded JN‑25, a complex secret code used by Japan to plan naval operations. After decoding a message about an attack on Midway Island, an important American refueling base halfway between North America and Asia, U.S. forces secretly moved three battleships to the region.
The

began at dawn on June 4, 1942, when Japanese planes attacked and damaged the U.S. base on the island. After the initial attack, Japanese scout planes spotted the U.S. ships, but the U.S. began bombing the Japanese fleet before they could respond. U.S. forces pursued the retreating Navy and inflicted further damage, bringing an end to Japan's expansion in the Pacific Theater.

contents.text: After months of Japanese successes, the tide began to turn in favor of the United States in the Pacific Theater in mid-1942. Read the passage on developments in the Pacific Theater in 1942. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: In early 1942, U.S.

, or codebreakers, decoded JN‑25, a complex secret code used by Japan to plan naval operations. After decoding a message about an attack on Midway Island, an important American refueling base halfway between North America and Asia, U.S. forces secretly moved three battleships to the region.
The

began at dawn on June 4, 1942, when Japanese planes attacked and damaged the U.S. base on the island. After the initial attack, Japanese scout planes spotted the U.S. ships, but the U.S. began bombing the Japanese fleet before they could respond. Japan's four largest ships at Midway were hit by U.S. bombers on the first day of battle and quickly sunk. Without its largest ships, the Japanese Navy was forced to retreat from Midway. U.S. forces pursued the retreating Navy and inflicted further damage, bringing an end to Japan's expansion in the Pacific Theater.

explanationText.text: The list shows that, from 1937 to 1938, the United States experienced an economic downturn during its recovery from the Great Depression. So, the nation had not fully recovered from the Great Depression when World War II began in 1939.

content.text: Before the Pearl Harbor attack, the United States had not prepared for or contributed to any part of World War II.

explanationText.text: The list shows the opposite. It shows that, in September 1940, President Roosevelt instituted the first peacetime U.S. military draft, and in March 1941, the U.S. began supplying weapons to the United Kingdom through the Lend-Lease Act. So, the United States began preparing for World War II before the Pearl Harbor attack on December 7, 1941.

pieces.text: The federal government actively mobilized the nation for war, spending over $321 billion—and increasing the national debt by
billion—from 1941 to 1945. This was more than twice what the government had spent in the nation's entire history before the war.

contents.text: This mobilization was necessary in order to meet the nation's wartime needs. Match each wartime need to the government action that addressed it.

draggableItems.text: The government raised taxes on businesses, expanded income taxes, and borrowed money from citizens using war bonds.
The government created the Office of Price Administration to set agricultural prices, wages, and rents nationwide.
By encouraging enlistment and expanding the draft, the government added 13 million new military service members during the war.
The government set up the War Production Board to shift U.S. factories toward war production.
The government encouraged women and minority group members to join the industrial workforce, which grew by over 10 million workers during the war.

staticItems.text: To fight a global war, the U.S. military needed more war supplies, such as armor, planes, vehicles, and weapons.
To maintain economic stability during the war, the government needed to manage shortages and prevent huge price jumps.
To meet wartime production goals and replace workers who joined the military, the nation needed millions more full-time workers.
To pay for war spending and debts, the U.S. government needed new sources of funding.
To have enough service members to fight in the war, the U.S. government needed millions more people to join the armed forces.

contents.text: To help mobilize for the war, the U.S. government spent billions of dollars on military research and development. This funding was used for scientific advancements and technological innovations that profoundly affected the war. Match each advancement or innovation to its outcome.

draggableItems.text: U.S. officers deciphered a Japanese coded communication system, giving the Allies advance knowledge of enemy plans.
U.S. industry quickly manufactured the medicine to treat soldiers, saving many lives on the battlefield.
U.S. planes could more accurately reach their targets in German industrial areas even when they could not see the ground.
U.S. operators could detect enemy vessels at great distances, giving them tactical advantages over Germany and Japan.
U.S. bombers were less likely to be shot down by enemy airplanes, allowing for highly effective bombing campaigns.

staticItems.text: U.S. engineers developed the B‑17F bomber aircraft, which could carry massive bombs while flying higher than enemy aircraft could.
U.S. scientists developed new techniques to produce large amounts of penicillin, a highly effective antibiotic for treating infections.
U.S. engineers developed an electronic navigation system, allowing military pilots to plot their exact flight paths, even at night or in bad weather.
U.S. researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology developed advanced radar systems to locate distant airplanes or ships.
U.S. military intelligence developed the Magic project to intercept, decode, and evaluate secret enemy messages.

During the war, the U.S. government invested billions of dollars in U.S. infrastructure and industry, usually in the form of military defense contracts. For example, the government invested
billion to build factories, highways, military facilities, and power plants on the West Coast. Government wartime investment had profound effects on where U.S. citizens lived.

contents.text: Read the following passage about wartime migration caused by government industrial investment. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: During the war, around 15 million Americans moved to new residences. Some military personnel moved their families to military bases, while many other people moved for work in defense industry jobs. California had the largest share of government investment, and it also experienced the most wartime migration as
million people moved there. Industrial states like Illinois, Michigan, New York, and Ohio also experienced increases in both federal spending and people migrating from other states.

textContent.text: Defense industry jobs attracted diverse groups of people to urban areas, which grew rapidly during the war. Over 1 million African American people moved from the rural South to urban areas in the North and West as part of what historians call the Second Great Migration. Many Mexican American people also moved to cities during the war, as many industrial jobs were open to them for the first time. Industrial work also drew people from rural areas and Native American people from reservations.

explanationText.text: The list shows U.S. industrial production increased significantly after the Lend-Lease Act was passed in March 1941. So, producing war weapons helped the U.S. economy even before the nation entered the war in December 1941.

explanationText.text: The list shows that, from 1937 to 1938, the United States experienced an economic downturn during its recovery from the Great Depression. It also shows that, in March 1941, U.S. unemployment still remained significantly higher than normal. So, the nation had not fully recovered from the Great Depression when World War II began in 1939.

pieces.text: The federal government actively mobilized the nation for war, spending over $321 billion—and increasing the national debt by
billion—from 1941 to 1945. This was more than twice what the government had spent in the nation's entire history before the war.

contents.text: This mobilization was necessary in order to meet the nation's wartime needs. Match each wartime need to the government action that addressed it.

draggableItems.text: To fight a global war, the U.S. military needed more war supplies, such as armor, planes, vehicles, and weapons.
To pay for war spending and debts, the U.S. government needed new sources of funding.
To meet wartime production goals and replace workers who joined the military, the nation needed millions more full-time workers.
To have enough service members to fight in the war, the U.S. government needed millions more people to join the armed forces.
To maintain economic stability during the war, the government needed to manage shortages and prevent huge price jumps.

staticItems.text: The government created the Office of Price Administration to set agricultural prices, wages, and rents nationwide.
The government encouraged women and minority group members to join the industrial workforce, which grew by over 10 million workers during the war.
The government set up the War Production Board to shift U.S. factories toward war production.
By encouraging enlistment and expanding the draft, the government added 13 million new military service members during the war.
The government raised taxes on businesses, expanded income taxes, and borrowed money from citizens using war bonds.

contents.text: To help mobilize for the war, the U.S. government spent billions of dollars on military research and development. This funding was used for scientific advancements and technological innovations that profoundly affected the war. Match each innovation to its effect on the war.

draggableItems.text: U.S. military intelligence developed the Magic project to intercept, decode, and evaluate secret enemy messages.
U.S. manufacturers applied mass-production techniques developed in civilian car factories to the production of military vehicles.
U.S. scientists developed new techniques to produce large amounts of penicillin, a highly effective antibiotic for treating infections.
U.S. researchers at the Naval Research Laboratory developed advanced sonar systems to detect underwater vessels.
U.S. engineers developed the Sikorsky R-4, the world's first mass-produced military helicopter.

staticItems.text: U.S. officers deciphered a Japanese coded communication system, giving the Allies advance knowledge of enemy plans.
U.S. military pilots could carry supplies and troops to the battlefield and evacuate injured soldiers from dangerous or remote areas.
U.S. Navy ships could more accurately find and attack German submarines, helping the Allies win the Battle of the Atlantic.
U.S. industry quickly manufactured the medicine to treat soldiers, saving many lives on the battlefield.
U.S. industry made significantly more aircraft, naval ships, and tanks than the Axis powers combined, giving the Allies a major supply advantage.

During the war, the U.S. government invested billions of dollars in U.S. infrastructure and industry, usually in the form of military defense contracts. For example, the government invested
billion to build factories, highways, military facilities, and power plants on the West Coast. Government wartime investment had profound effects on where U.S. citizens lived.

contents.text: Read the following passage about wartime migration caused by government industrial investment. Then follow the instructions below.

pieces.text: During the war, around 15 million Americans moved to new residences. Some military personnel moved their families to military bases, while many other people moved for work in defense industry jobs. California had the largest share of government investment, and it also experienced the most wartime migration as
million people moved there. Industrial states like Illinois, Michigan, New York, and Ohio also experienced increases in both federal spending and people migrating from other states.

textContent.text: Defense industry jobs attracted diverse groups of people to urban areas, which grew rapidly during the war. Over 1 million African American people moved from the rural South to urban areas in the North and West as part of what historians call the Second Great Migration. Many Mexican American people also moved to cities during the war, as many industrial jobs were open to them for the first time. Industrial work also drew people from rural areas and Native American people from reservations.

contents.text: Look back at the list. These choices are correct:

content.text: To fight the war after the Pearl Harbor attack, presidential authority increased significantly.

explanationText.text: The list shows Congress significantly expanded President Roosevelt's wartime powers on December 18, 1941. So, presidential authority increased after the Pearl Harbor attack on December 7, 1941.

content.text: When World War II began, the United States had still not fully recovered from the Great Depression.

explanationText.text: The list shows that, from 1937 to 1938, the United States experienced an economic downturn during its recovery from the Great Depression. It also shows that, in March 1941, U.S. unemployment still remained significantly higher than normal. So, the nation had not fully recovered from the Great Depression when World War II began in 1939.

content.text: World War II had some positive effects on the U.S. economy even before the United States entered the war.

explanationText.text: The list shows U.S. industrial production increased significantly after the Lend-Lease Act was passed in March 1941. So, producing war weapons helped the U.S. economy even before the nation entered the war in December 1941.

contents.text: This choice is not correct:

content.text: Before the Pearl Harbor attack, the United States had not prepared for or contributed to any part of World War II.

explanationText.text: The list shows the opposite. It shows that, in September 1940, President Roosevelt instituted the first peacetime U.S. military draft, and in March 1941, the U.S. began supplying weapons to the United Kingdom through the Lend-Lease Act. So, the United States began preparing for World War II before the Pearl Harbor attack on December 7, 1941.

pieces.text: The federal government actively mobilized the nation for war, spending over $321 billion—and increasing the national debt by
billion—from 1941 to 1945. This was more than twice what the government had spent in the nation's entire history before the war.

contents.text: This mobilization was necessary in order to meet the nation's wartime needs. Match each wartime need to the government action that addressed it.

draggableItems.text: The government encouraged women and minority group members to join the industrial workforce, which grew by over 10 million workers during the war.
By encouraging enlistment and expanding the draft, the government added 13 million new military service members during the war.
The government set up the War Production Board to shift U.S. factories toward war production.
The government raised taxes on businesses, expanded income taxes, and borrowed money from citizens using war bonds.
The government created the Office of Price Administration to set agricultural prices, wages, and rents nationwide.

staticItems.text: To maintain economic stability during the war, the government needed to manage shortages and prevent huge price jumps.
To pay for war spending and debts, the U.S. government needed new sources of funding.
To fight a global war, the U.S. military needed more war supplies, such as armor, planes, vehicles, and weapons.
To have enough service members to fight in the war, the U.S. government needed millions more people to join the armed forces.
To meet wartime production goals and replace workers who joined the military, the nation needed millions more full-time workers.

draggableItems.text: U.S. officers deciphered a Japanese coded communication system, giving the Allies advance knowledge of enemy plans.
U.S. operators could detect enemy vessels at great distances, giving them tactical advantages over Germany and Japan.
U.S. bombers were less likely to be shot down by enemy airplanes, allowing for highly effective bombing campaigns.
U.S. planes could more accurately reach their targets in German industrial areas even when they could not see the ground.
U.S. industry quickly manufactured the medicine to treat soldiers, saving many lives on the battlefield.

staticItems.text: U.S. scientists developed new techniques to produce large amounts of penicillin, a highly effective antibiotic for treating infections.
U.S. military intelligence developed the Magic project to intercept, decode, and evaluate secret enemy messages.
U.S. researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology developed advanced radar systems to locate distant airplanes or ships.
U.S. engineers developed the B‑17F bomber aircraft, which could carry massive bombs while flying higher than enemy aircraft could.
U.S. engineers developed an electronic navigation system, allowing military pilots to plot their exact flight paths, even at night or in bad weather.

During the war, the U.S. government invested billions of dollars in U.S. infrastructure and industry, usually in the form of military defense contracts. For example, the government invested
billion to build factories, highways, military facilities, and power plants on the West Coast. Government wartime investment had profound effects on where U.S. citizens lived.

contents.text: Read the following passage about wartime migration caused by government industrial investment. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: During the war, around 15 million Americans moved to new residences. Some military personnel moved their families to military bases, while many other people moved for work in defense industry jobs. California had the largest share of government investment, and it also experienced the most wartime migration as
million people moved there. Industrial states like Illinois, Michigan, New York, and Ohio also experienced increases in both federal spending and people migrating from other states.

textContent.text: Defense industry jobs attracted diverse groups of people to urban areas, which grew rapidly during the war. Over 1 million African American people moved from the rural South to urban areas in the North and West as part of what historians call the Second Great Migration. Many Mexican American people also moved to cities during the war, as many industrial jobs were open to them for the first time. Industrial work also drew people from rural areas and Native American people from reservations.

pieces.text: Which of the following are outcomes of government wartime investment? Select

choices.text: States that received more federal investment tended to draw more migrants.
Rural areas attracted most of the migrants looking for work in defense industries.
People from diverse backgrounds found urban industrial work, often for the first time.
States in the North and West received little government funding, so they drew few migrants.

contents.text: Government wartime investment led to profound increases in production, employment, migration, and urban populations during the war. The booming wartime economy finally brought the nation out of the Great Depression. Despite this prosperity, there were signs of economic hardship.

Average workers' wages grew by 35 percent during the war, with some wages increasing 100 percent or more.
Construction companies focused on building wartime factories over new homes, so many cities experienced housing shortages.

contents.text: Look back at the list. These choices are correct:

content.text: The United States began preparing for and contributing to World War II even before the Pearl Harbor attack.

explanationText.text: The list shows that, in September 1940, President Roosevelt instituted the first peacetime U.S. military draft, and in March 1941, the U.S. began supplying weapons to the United Kingdom through the Lend-Lease Act. So, the United States began preparing for World War II before the Pearl Harbor attack on December 7, 1941.

content.text: The United States had still not fully recovered from the Great Depression when World War II began.

explanationText.text: The list shows that, from 1937 to 1938, the United States experienced an economic downturn during its recovery from the Great Depression. It also shows that, in March 1941, U.S. unemployment still remained significantly higher than normal. So, the nation had not fully recovered from the Great Depression when World War II began in 1939.

content.text: Even before the United States entered World War II, the war had some positive effects on the U.S. economy.

explanationText.text: The list shows U.S. industrial production increased significantly after the Lend-Lease Act was passed in March 1941. So, producing war weapons helped the U.S. economy even before the nation entered the war in December 1941.

contents.text: This choice is not correct:

content.text: Congress took command of the war effort after the Pearl Harbor attack, significantly limiting the president's role.

explanationText.text: The list shows the opposite. Congress significantly expanded President Roosevelt's wartime powers on December 18, 1941. So, presidential authority increased after the Pearl Harbor attacks on December 7, 1941.

pieces.text: The federal government actively mobilized the nation for war, spending over $321 billion—and increasing the national debt by
billion—from 1941 to 1945. This was more than twice what the government had spent in the nation's entire history before the war.

contents.text: This mobilization was necessary in order to meet the nation's wartime needs. Match each wartime need to the government action that addressed it.

draggableItems.text: To maintain economic stability during the war, the government needed to manage shortages and prevent huge price jumps.
To meet wartime production goals and replace workers who joined the military, the nation needed millions more full-time workers.
To pay for war spending and debts, the U.S. government needed new sources of funding.
To have enough service members to fight in the war, the U.S. government needed millions more people to join the armed forces.
To fight a global war, the U.S. military needed more war supplies, such as armor, planes, vehicles, and weapons.

staticItems.text: The government encouraged women and minority group members to join the industrial workforce, which grew by over 10 million workers during the war.
The government set up the War Production Board to shift U.S. factories toward war production.
By encouraging enlistment and expanding the draft, the government added 13 million new military service members during the war.
The government created the Office of Price Administration to set agricultural prices, wages, and rents nationwide.
The government raised taxes on businesses, expanded income taxes, and borrowed money from citizens using war bonds.

billion to build factories, highways, military facilities, and power plants on the West Coast. Government wartime investment had profound effects on where U.S. citizens lived.

contents.text: Read the following passage about wartime migration caused by government industrial investment. Then follow the instructions below.

pieces.text: During the war, around 15 million Americans moved to new residences. Some military personnel moved their families to military bases, while many other people moved for work in defense industry jobs. California had the largest share of government investment, and it also experienced the most wartime migration as
million people moved there. Industrial states like Illinois, Michigan, New York, and Ohio also experienced increases in both federal spending and people migrating from other states.

textContent.text: Defense industry jobs attracted diverse groups of people to urban areas, which grew rapidly during the war. Over 1 million African American people moved from the rural South to urban areas in the North and West as part of what historians call the Second Great Migration. Many Mexican American people also moved to cities during the war, as many industrial jobs were open to them for the first time. Industrial work also drew people from rural areas and Native American people from reservations.

As the nation mobilized for war, many political and military leaders believed that Japanese Americans were a threat to the United States. They pressured President Franklin Roosevelt to remove all people of Japanese ancestry, including U.S. citizens, from the Pacific Coast. On February 19, 1942, President Roosevelt issued
. Read excerpts from the order. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: Whereas the [success] of the war requires every possible protection against [spying] and against sabotage to national‐defense material, national‐defense premises, and national‐defense utilities…I hereby authorize and direct the Secretary of War, and the military commanders…to [identify] military areas in such places and of such extent as he or the appropriate military commander may determine, from which any or all persons may be excluded, and…the right of any person to enter, remain in, or leave shall be subject to whatever restrictions the Secretary of War or the appropriate military commander may impose in his discretion.

contents.text: Although Executive Order 9066 did not specifically mention Japanese people, it was immediately used by U.S. military leaders to target Japanese Americans. Based on the executive order, the U.S. government took steps to remove all Japanese Americans from the Pacific Coast. Match each action taken by the U.S. government to its effect on Japanese Americans.

draggableItems.text: Japanese Americans who disobey wartime military orders face up to a year in prison and a $5,000 fine.
Japanese Americans are forcibly removed from their homes. They must register at Civilian Control Stations before being sent to temporary "assembly centers."
Over 110,000 Japanese Americans, including 70,000 U.S. citizens, are sent to 10 permanent "relocation centers" in the interior of the United States.
Japanese Americans in the military areas have to remain in their homes from 8:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m.

staticItems.text: March 1, 1942: General John DeWitt issues Public Proclamation 1, which creates military areas covering large portions of four western states.
Japanese Americans living in one of the military areas are told they will be removed from their homes and are encouraged to voluntarily "evacuate" outside the area.
March 1, 1942: General DeWitt issues a curfew that applies only to the Japanese Americans living in the military areas.
March 20, 1942: Congress passes Public Law 503, which makes it illegal to violate military orders in the military areas.
March 24, 1942: General DeWitt issues the first of 108 civilian exclusion orders, which exclude all Japanese people, both U.S. citizens and noncitizens, from specific parts of the military areas.
May 26, 1942: The War Relocation Authority, created by President Roosevelt's Executive Order 9102, begins transporting people from the "assembly centers" to "relocation centers."

March 1, 1942: General DeWitt issues a curfew that applies only to the Japanese Americans living in the military areas.
March 20, 1942: Congress passes Public Law 503, which makes it illegal to violate military orders in the military areas.
March 24, 1942: General DeWitt issues the first of 108 civilian exclusion orders, which exclude all Japanese people, both U.S. citizens and noncitizens, from specific parts of the military areas.
May 26, 1942: The War Relocation Authority, created by President Roosevelt's Executive Order 9102, begins transporting people from the "assembly centers" to "relocation centers."

draggableItems.text: Japanese Americans who disobey wartime military orders face up to a year in prison and a $5,000 fine.
Japanese Americans are forcibly removed from their homes. They must register at Civilian Control Stations before being sent to temporary "assembly centers."
Over 110,000 Japanese Americans, including 70,000 U.S. citizens, are sent to 10 permanent "relocation centers" in the interior of the United States.
Japanese Americans in the military areas have to remain in their homes from 8:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m.

contents.text: The U.S. government's civilian exclusion orders gave Japanese Americans seven to ten days to prepare to leave their homes. Furthermore, they could only bring what they could carry with them. These limits created many personal, professional, and financial challenges for Japanese Americans. The following images show some of these challenges. Match each image with the correct description.

The camps with 10,000 to 15,000 people are Heart Mountain, Gila River and Manzanar. The camps with 5,000 to 10,000 people are Amache, Jerome, Minidoka, Rohwer, and Topaz.

contents.text: In the following excerpts, Frank Yamasaki describes his experiences as a young Japanese American man incarcerated at the Minidoka camp in Idaho. Read the excerpts. Then answer the question below.

content.text: [Minidoka] was very, very dusty…So you just, every time you take a step, you would just have a puff of smoke—I mean, of dust—and if you have even the slightest breeze…wow, you're in, like a fog. And when you go to the mess hall to eat, of course, when you chew the food, you can feel the grit of the sand…The early stage where the area was undeveloped and very dusty and the toilet facility was still poor.

I would say [our living quarters were] roughly 12 by 15 [feet] or so in size…And in each unit there would be a family. And each unit would have one large pot belly stove, cast iron stove…And my father and mother, they combined the three beds with [my younger brother] together so that all three of them could sleep in one area, and I had a bed and my brother had one. So there were five of us in this little room…

pieces.text: <citation>Yamasaki, Frank. "Frank Yamasaki Interview I." By Lori Hoshino and Stephen Fugita. Densho Digital Archive (Densho Visual History Collection, August 18, 1997).</citation>

content.text: Some [Japanese immigrants] have lost a lot more than others financially and what they lost was very difficult because they worked so hard. They scrimped and they saved their money…

And of course some [worked in the camps]. I'm sure a great number of them. People who used to make tofu and things, they would be, they would make tofu there. Others, who were farmers, would be working on the farm…I noticed that they seemed to pick [people] who were pretty strong looking and especially with a mustache, which gave them a feeling of authority, they were security guards…
I think the wages, monthly salary was between $6 and $8 for unskilled workers and $14 to $16 or so for skilled doctors and people like that…

pieces.text: <citation>Yamasaki, Frank. "Frank Yamasaki Interview I." By Lori Hoshino and Stephen Fugita. Densho Digital Archive (Densho Visual History Collection, August 18, 1997).</citation>
[My father] got involved in a lot of crafting. They would find scraps of wood, pieces of crate that were being discarded and they would carve things…I have a shrine,
, that he made…My mother even learned how to sing, they call it
. It's a kind of a guttural type of singing.

content.text: They had an orchestra called the Hawaiian Serenaders…And they used to play for dances, and they were so good that there is a town called Twin Falls, close to Minidoka, [where they] performed a western song on the radio there once a week…And, of course, in sport they had judo, sumo…They had boxing. They had, of course, basketball, football, just name it, they had just about all the sports.

pieces.text: <citation>Yamasaki, Frank. "Frank Yamasaki Interview I." By Lori Hoshino and Stephen Fugita. Densho Digital Archive (Densho Visual History Collection, August 18, 1997).</citation>

Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor intensified existing anti-Japanese discrimination among many people in the United States. Following the attack, the United States entered World War II against Japan, Germany, and Italy. As the nation mobilized for war, many political and military leaders believed that Japanese Americans were a threat to the United States. They pressured President Franklin Roosevelt to remove all people of Japanese ancestry, including U.S. citizens, from the Pacific Coast. On February 19, 1942, President Roosevelt issued
. Read excerpts from the order. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: Whereas the [success] of the war requires every possible protection against [spying] and against sabotage to national‐defense material, national‐defense premises, and national‐defense utilities…I hereby authorize and direct the Secretary of War, and the military commanders…to [identify] military areas in such places and of such extent as he or the appropriate military commander may determine, from which any or all persons may be excluded, and…the right of any person to enter, remain in, or leave shall be subject to whatever restrictions the Secretary of War or the appropriate military commander may impose in his discretion.

The Secretary of War is hereby authorized to provide for residents of any such area who are excluded there from, such transportation, food, shelter, and other accommodations as may be necessary…to accomplish the purpose of this order.

contents.text: Based on the excerpts, which of the following statements are true under Executive Order 9066? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Military commanders can create rules within military areas, such as setting up a curfew.
Military commanders can decide that certain places are "military areas" considered crucial to national security and defense.
Military commanders can only remove someone from a military area if that person is first charged, tried, and convicted of a crime.
Military commanders can ban certain people from military areas and use all necessary resources to remove people from those areas.

contents.text: Look back at the passage. These choices are correct:

content.text: Military commanders can create rules within military areas, such as setting up a curfew.

explanationText.text: The passage says that, within the military areas, the "right of any person to enter, remain in, or leave shall be subject to whatever restrictions," or rules, are created by military commanders. A curfew limits the hours when people can leave their homes, so it is a type of restriction.

content.text: Military commanders can decide that certain places are "military areas" considered crucial to national security and defense.

explanationText.text: The passage says that, because success in the war requires protection against spying and sabotage, military commanders are authorized to identify military areas that certain people can be excluded from. Sabotage means causing damage for military or political reasons.

content.text: Military commanders can ban certain people from military areas and use all necessary resources to remove people from those areas.

explanationText.text: The passage says that military commanders can designate military areas "from which any or all persons may be excluded." Banning people is a form of excluding them. The passage says that military commanders are authorized to use "such transportation, food, shelter, and other accommodations as may be necessary" to remove certain people from the military areas.

contents.text: The other choice is not correct:

content.text: Military commanders can only remove someone from a military area if that person is first charged, tried, and convicted of a crime.

explanationText.text: The passage says that military commanders can determine whether "any or all persons may be excluded" from the military areas. The passage does not say that people who are excluded, or removed, must first face a criminal justice process.

contents.text: The U.S. government's civilian exclusion orders gave Japanese Americans seven to ten days to prepare to leave their homes. Furthermore, they could only bring what they could carry with them. These limits created many personal, professional, and financial challenges for Japanese Americans. The following images show some of these challenges. Match each image with the correct description.

imageCaption.text: A store owned by Japanese Americans offers up to 50 percent off its items.
A Japanese American man boards up a hayloft on his farm prior to removal.
A Japanese American woman picks strawberries on her farm a few days before removal.
Japanese American property is vandalized while being stored in a local business.

innerComponent.text: Japanese American property that was left behind was often stolen or damaged, since the owners were not there to protect it.
Japanese American farmers did not know when they would be able to return, so many shut down their farms.
Some Japanese Americans found renters to watch their land, but renters sometimes ignored the crops and stole property.
Many Japanese American business owners had to sell their goods at a steep discount before leaving.

contents.text: In the following excerpts, Frank Yamasaki describes his experiences as a young Japanese American man incarcerated at the Minidoka camp in Idaho. Read the excerpts. Then answer the question below.

content.text: [Minidoka] was very, very dusty…So you just, every time you take a step, you would just have a puff of smoke—I mean, of dust—and if you have even the slightest breeze…wow, you're in, like a fog. And when you go to the mess hall to eat, of course, when you chew the food, you can feel the grit of the sand…The early stage where the area was undeveloped and very dusty and the toilet facility was still poor.

I would say [our living quarters were] roughly 12 by 15 [feet] or so in size…And in each unit there would be a family. And each unit would have one large pot belly stove, cast iron stove…And my father and mother, they combined the three beds with [my younger brother] together so that all three of them could sleep in one area, and I had a bed and my brother had one. So there were five of us in this little room…

pieces.text: <citation>Yamasaki, Frank. "Frank Yamasaki Interview I." By Lori Hoshino and Stephen Fugita. Densho Digital Archive (Densho Visual History Collection, August 18, 1997).</citation>

content.text: Some [Japanese immigrants] have lost a lot more than others financially and what they lost was very difficult because they worked so hard. They scrimped and they saved their money…

And of course some [worked in the camps]. I'm sure a great number of them. People who used to make tofu and things, they would be, they would make tofu there. Others, who were farmers, would be working on the farm…I noticed that they seemed to pick [people] who were pretty strong looking and especially with a mustache, which gave them a feeling of authority, they were security guards…
I think the wages, monthly salary was between $6 and $8 for unskilled workers and $14 to $16 or so for skilled doctors and people like that…

pieces.text: <citation>Yamasaki, Frank. "Frank Yamasaki Interview I." By Lori Hoshino and Stephen Fugita. Densho Digital Archive (Densho Visual History Collection, August 18, 1997).</citation>
[My father] got involved in a lot of crafting. They would find scraps of wood, pieces of crate that were being discarded and they would carve things…I have a shrine,
, that he made…My mother even learned how to sing, they call it
. It's a kind of a guttural type of singing.

content.text: They had an orchestra called the Hawaiian Serenaders…And they used to play for dances, and they were so good that there is a town called Twin Falls, close to Minidoka, [where they] performed a western song on the radio there once a week…And, of course, in sport they had judo, sumo…They had boxing. They had, of course, basketball, football, just name it, they had just about all the sports.

contents.text: While incarcerated, many Japanese Americans tried to avoid conflict and build community in the camps. However, their incarceration included many forms of persecution, which some Japanese Americans resisted. Match each form of persecution to the way Japanese Americans resisted it.

draggableItems.text: The War Relocation Authority required all Japanese Americans to fill out a "loyalty questionnaire" to prove their loyalty to the United States.
The U.S. government forcibly removed all Japanese Americans on the West Coast from their homes and incarcerated them in camps without charges or trials.
The U.S. government drafted thousands of young Japanese American men in the camps to serve in the U.S. military during World War II.
Camp leaders often forced Japanese Americans to help build the camps that incarcerated them. Inmates had poor living quarters, dangerous work settings, and very low wages.

staticItems.text: Multiple Japanese Americans challenged their removal and incarceration in court, arguing that their constitutional rights had been violated.
Thousands of Japanese Americans refused to fill out the form. Some U.S. citizens promised to be loyal only if the U.S. respected their rights.
Japanese Americans organized for better living and working conditions. They used strikes and elected representatives to negotiate with camp leaders.
Nearly 300 Japanese Americans refused to report for the draft, and many were charged with draft evasion and imprisoned in federal prisons.

contents.text: At the time of the Pearl Harbor attacks, Japanese people had been living and working in the United States for over 50 years. The timeline below provides information about Japanese experiences in the United States before World War II. Look at the timeline. Then follow the instructions below.

alternativeText.text: A timeline that includes the following items: 1891: The first Japanese immigrants come to the U.S., mostly working as agricultural laborers in California. 1894: A U.S. court rules that Japanese immigrants cannot become U.S. citizens because they are not "free white [people]." Early 1900s: Japanese people begin building communities on the West Coast, including starting businesses and Japanese-language schools. 1913: A California law bans Japanese immigrants from owning land. 1920: Japanese Americans make up two percent of California's population, yet they produce more than ten percent of the state's crop value. 1924: The Immigration Act of 1924 nearly ends Japanese immigration to the United States. 1928: James Sakamoto of Seattle starts the Japanese American Courier, an English-language newspaper.

Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor intensified existing anti-Japanese discrimination among many people in the United States. Following the attack, the United States entered World War II against Japan, Germany, and Italy. As the nation mobilized for war, many political and military leaders believed that Japanese Americans were a threat to the United States. They pressured President Franklin Roosevelt to remove all people of Japanese ancestry, including U.S. citizens, from the Pacific Coast. On February 19, 1942, President Roosevelt issued
. Read excerpts from the order. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: Whereas the [success] of the war requires every possible protection against [spying] and against sabotage to national‐defense material, national‐defense premises, and national‐defense utilities…I hereby authorize and direct the Secretary of War, and the military commanders…to [identify] military areas in such places and of such extent as he or the appropriate military commander may determine, from which any or all persons may be excluded, and…the right of any person to enter, remain in, or leave shall be subject to whatever restrictions the Secretary of War or the appropriate military commander may impose in his discretion.

The Secretary of War is hereby authorized to provide for residents of any such area who are excluded there from, such transportation, food, shelter, and other accommodations as may be necessary…to accomplish the purpose of this order.

under Executive Order 9066:

elements.text: The passage says that military commanders are authorized to use "such transportation, food, shelter, and other accommodations as may be necessary" to remove certain people from the military areas.

content.text: Military commanders can ban certain people from military areas.

elements.text: The passage says that military commanders can designate military areas "from which any or all persons may be excluded." Banning people is a form of excluding them.

content.text: Military commanders can decide that certain places are "military areas" considered crucial to national security and defense.

elements.text: The passage says that, because success in the war requires protection against spying and sabotage, military commanders are authorized to identify military areas that certain people can be excluded from. Sabotage means causing damage for military or political reasons.

elements.text: The passage says that, within the military areas, the "right of any person to enter, remain in, or leave shall be subject to whatever restrictions," or rules, are created by military commanders. A curfew limits the hours when people can leave their homes, so it is a type of restriction.

contents.text: Although Executive Order 9066 did not specifically mention Japanese people, it was immediately used by U.S. military leaders to target Japanese Americans. Based on the executive order, the U.S. government took steps to remove all Japanese Americans from the Pacific Coast. Match each action taken by the U.S. government to its effect on Japanese Americans.

draggableItems.text: Japanese Americans who disobey wartime military orders face up to a year in prison and a $5,000 fine.
Japanese Americans are forcibly removed from their homes. They must register at Civilian Control Stations before being sent to temporary "assembly centers."
Japanese Americans in the military areas have to remain in their homes from 8:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m.
Over 110,000 Japanese Americans, including 70,000 U.S. citizens, are sent to 10 permanent "relocation centers" in the interior of the United States.

staticItems.text: March 1, 1942: General John DeWitt issues Public Proclamation 1, which creates military areas covering large portions of four western states.
Japanese Americans living in one of the military areas are told they will be removed from their homes and are encouraged to voluntarily "evacuate" outside the area.

March 20, 1942: Congress passes Public Law 503, which makes it illegal to violate military orders in the military areas.
March 24, 1942: General DeWitt issues the first of 108 civilian exclusion orders, which exclude all Japanese people, both U.S. citizens and noncitizens, from specific parts of the military areas.

contents.text: The U.S. government's civilian exclusion orders gave Japanese Americans seven to ten days to prepare to leave their homes. contents.text: In the following excerpts, Frank Yamasaki describes his experiences as a young Japanese American man incarcerated at the Minidoka camp in Idaho. Read the excerpts. Then answer the question below.

content.text: [Minidoka] was very, very dusty…So you just, every time you take a step, you would just have a puff of smoke—I mean, of dust—and if you have even the slightest breeze…wow, you're in, like a fog. And when you go to the mess hall to eat, of course, when you chew the food, you can feel the grit of the sand…The early stage where the area was undeveloped and very dusty and the toilet facility was still poor.

I would say [our living quarters were] roughly 12 by 15 [feet] or so in size…And in each unit there would be a family. And each unit would have one large pot belly stove, cast iron stove…And my father and mother, they combined the three beds with [my younger brother] together so that all three of them could sleep in one area, and I had a bed and my brother had one. So there were five of us in this little room…

pieces.text: <citation>Yamasaki, Frank. "Frank Yamasaki Interview I." By Lori Hoshino and Stephen Fugita. Densho Digital Archive (Densho Visual History Collection, August 18, 1997).</citation>

content.text: Some [Japanese immigrants] have lost a lot more than others financially and what they lost was very difficult because they worked so hard. They scrimped and they saved their money…

And of course some [worked in the camps]. I'm sure a great number of them. People who used to make tofu and things, they would be, they would make tofu there. Others, who were farmers, would be working on the farm…I noticed that they seemed to pick [people] who were pretty strong looking and especially with a mustache, which gave them a feeling of authority, they were security guards…
I think the wages, monthly salary was between $6 and $8 for unskilled workers and $14 to $16 or so for skilled doctors and people like that…

pieces.text: <citation>Yamasaki, Frank. "Frank Yamasaki Interview I." By Lori Hoshino and Stephen Fugita. Densho Digital Archive (Densho Visual History Collection, August 18, 1997).</citation>
[My father] got involved in a lot of crafting. They would find scraps of wood, pieces of crate that were being discarded and they would carve things…I have a shrine,
, that he made…My mother even learned how to sing, they call it
. It's a kind of a guttural type of singing.

content.text: They had an orchestra called the Hawaiian Serenaders…And they used to play for dances, and they were so good that there is a town called Twin Falls, close to Minidoka, [where they] performed a western song on the radio there once a week…And, of course, in sport they had judo, sumo…They had boxing. They had, of course, basketball, football, just name it, they had just about all the sports.

Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor intensified existing anti-Japanese discrimination among many people in the United States. Following the attack, the United States entered World War II against Japan, Germany, and Italy. As the nation mobilized for war, many political and military leaders believed that Japanese Americans were a threat to the United States. They pressured President Franklin Roosevelt to remove all people of Japanese ancestry, including U.S. citizens, from the Pacific Coast. On February 19, 1942, President Roosevelt issued
. Read excerpts from the order. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: Whereas the [success] of the war requires every possible protection against [spying] and against sabotage to national‐defense material, national‐defense premises, and national‐defense utilities…I hereby authorize and direct the Secretary of War, and the military commanders…to [identify] military areas in such places and of such extent as he or the appropriate military commander may determine, from which any or all persons may be excluded, and…the right of any person to enter, remain in, or leave shall be subject to whatever restrictions the Secretary of War or the appropriate military commander may impose in his discretion.

The Secretary of War is hereby authorized to provide for residents of any such area who are excluded there from, such transportation, food, shelter, and other accommodations as may be necessary…to accomplish the purpose of this order.

choices.text: Military commanders can create rules within military areas, such as setting up a curfew.
Military commanders can only remove someone from a military area if that person is first charged, tried, and convicted of a crime.

contents.text: Look back at the passage. These choices are correct:

content.text: Military commanders can create rules within military areas, such as setting up a curfew.

explanationText.text: The passage says that, within the military areas, the "right of any person to enter, remain in, or leave shall be subject to whatever restrictions," or rules, are created by military commanders. A curfew limits the hours when people can leave their homes, so it is a type of restriction.

content.text: Military commanders can ban certain people from military areas and use all necessary resources to remove people from those areas.

explanationText.text: The passage says that military commanders can designate military areas "from which any or all persons may be excluded." Banning people is a form of excluding them. The passage says that military commanders are authorized to use "such transportation, food, shelter, and other accommodations as may be necessary" to remove certain people from the military areas.

content.text: Military commanders can decide that certain places are "military areas" considered crucial to national security and defense.

explanationText.text: The passage says that, because success in the war requires protection against spying and sabotage, military commanders are authorized to identify military areas that certain people can be excluded from. Sabotage means causing damage for military or political reasons.

contents.text: The other choice is not correct:

content.text: Military commanders can only remove someone from a military area if that person is first charged, tried, and convicted of a crime.

explanationText.text: The passage says that military commanders can determine whether "any or all persons may be excluded" from the military areas. The passage does not say that people who are excluded, or removed, must first face a criminal justice process.

contents.text: The U.S. government's civilian exclusion orders gave Japanese Americans seven to ten days to prepare to leave their homes. Furthermore, they could only bring what they could carry with them. These limits created many personal, professional, and financial challenges for Japanese Americans. The following images show some of these challenges. Match each image with the correct description.

imageCaption.text: A store owned by Japanese Americans offers up to 50 percent off its items.
A Japanese American man boards up a hayloft on his farm prior to removal.
A Japanese American woman picks strawberries on her farm a few days before removal.
Japanese American property is vandalized while being stored in a local business.

innerComponent.text: Some Japanese Americans found renters to watch their land, but renters sometimes ignored the crops and stole property.
Japanese American farmers did not know when they would be able to return, so many shut down their farms.
Many Japanese American business owners had to sell their goods at a steep discount before leaving.
Japanese American property that was left behind was often stolen or damaged, since the owners were not there to protect it.

alternativeText.text: This map shows incarceration camps in the United States. The military exclusion area includes all of California and parts of Washington state, Oregon, and Arizona. There are four camps in the exclusion area. There are six other camps, mostly located in the Mountain West region of the U.S. The camps with 15,000 to 20,000 people are Poston and Tule Lake. The camps with 10,000 to 15,000 people are Heart Mountain, Gila River and Manzanar. The camps with 5,000 to 10,000 people are Amache, Jerome, Minidoka, Rohwer, and Topaz.
